_metadata.rubric: owner-clarified rubric with calibration anchors + no-literal-false-facts reminder, 2026-10-18
_metadata.independence: I read only u25-blind-input.json; no other file, search, web or API was consulted.

hints.reason: IRON via the phrase 'iron jaw' (a tough chin), WOLF via the animal's famous jaws; the iron side is idiomatic and may not surface.
IRON via the heavy iron-jawed trap, WOLF via the wolf trap it is set for; one shared scene.
IRON via wrought-iron fence is solid, but WOLF only reaches a fence as something it might be kept out by, which is filler.

best_available.why: The iron wolf trap is a single recognizable object that names both words.

pairs.pair_note: TRAP carries the pair; JAW is a usable second route if the 'iron jaw' idiom is acceptable.

hints.reason: KEY via lock and key is immediate, but nothing connects LOCK to KING.
Contains the target KING as a substring, and KEY has no route to it anyway.
KING via the crown is obvious; KEY has no natural link to a crown.
KING via the castle he rules from, KEY via 'keys to the castle'; the key side is a phrase rather than an object a player sees first.

best_available.why: Only hint that reaches both words, through the king's seat and the 'keys to the castle' phrase.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; the pair is hard because KEY and KING share little beyond castles and chess. CASTLE is the only serviceable hint.

hints.reason: KNIGHT via suit of armor is immediate; KEY has no route to armor.
KNIGHT via the castle he defends, KEY via 'keys to the castle' or the castle gate key; the key side is thinner.
KEY via a locked treasure chest is good, but KNIGHT reaches CHEST only via the breastplate, which players will not see as a knight link.

best_available.why: The castle is where knights live and the one object players also associate with keys.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; CASTLE is the only hint touching both sides.

hints.reason: KEY via house key, LIGHT via lighthouse; both compounds are everyday words.
Verb route: you turn a key and turn on a light.
LIGHT via photography/photons, KEY via the 'key light' term of studio lighting; both routes need an explanation.

best_available.why: House key and lighthouse are two broad compounds pointing cleanly at each word.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; HOUSE and TURN both pass comfortably, PHOTO is a photographer's in-joke.

hints.reason: LION via the zoo is immediate; KEY has no route to a zoo.
LION via the lion's cage, KEY via the key that locks the cage; the key side is plausible but secondary.

best_available.why: A locked lion cage is a scene that includes a key, even if the key is not the first thing seen.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; CAGE is a fair stretch, ZOO is purely one-sided.

hints.reason: KEY via a musical key change, MOON via its changing phases; both links are real but neither is a strong first association.
KEY via keystone, MOON via moonstone; two established compounds.
KEY via piano keys is immediate, MOON via the Moonlight Sonata or Clair de Lune is a recognizable but indirect cultural route.

best_available.why: Keystone and moonstone are both common compounds.

pairs.pair_note: STONE is clean; PIANO is a defensible second if the Moonlight Sonata route is accepted.

hints.reason: MOUSE via mouse click, KEY via the click of a key being pressed or turned; shared computer desk scene.
MOUSE sits on the desk; KEY reaches a desk via the keys on the keyboard or a desk-drawer key, both secondary.
Contains the target KEY as a substring, so it is a rule failure despite the obvious mouse-and-keyboard link.
Computer mouse and computer keys both belong to the same device.

best_available.why: Everyone pictures a computer with keys and a mouse.

pairs.pair_note: Easy pair; KEYBOARD must be dropped on the substring rule.

hints.reason: NIGHT via a night curfew is clear; KEY reaches it only through being locked out, which is invented filler.
KEY via lock and key is immediate; NIGHT via locking up at night is a weak habitual link.
KEY via the hotel room key or key card, NIGHT via hotels being booked by the night.

best_available.why: A hotel stay naturally includes both a room key and a count of nights.

pairs.pair_note: HOTEL is the only passing hint; LOCK leans heavily on KEY.

hints.reason: KEY as a small low island (the Florida Keys), OCEAN as what surrounds an island.
KEY via the Florida Keys, OCEAN via the Atlantic coast of Florida; geography route.
KEY via Key West is strong, but OCEAN reaches WEST only through Key West itself being on the water.

best_available.why: Florida Keys plus Florida's ocean coast is the most broadly known combination.

pairs.pair_note: Geography pair that works; WEST depends on the same Key West fact for both sides.

hints.reason: PIRATE via pirate treasure is immediate, KEY via the key to the locked treasure chest; the key side is part of the same scene.
KEY via the locked chest, PIRATE via the pirate's treasure chest.
PIRATE via 'dead men tell no tales' or Dead Man's Chest is a thin cultural link, and KEY reaches DEAD only via the typist's 'dead key' or a film plot detail.

best_available.why: A pirate's locked treasure chest is one picture containing both targets.

pairs.pair_note: CHEST and TREASURE both work through the same scene; DEAD does not reach KEY.

hints.reason: KEY via the ceremonial key to the city, QUEEN via the 'Queen City' nickname (Cincinnati, Charlotte); the queen side is regional.
QUEEN via Freddie Mercury is strong; KEY has no route to Freddie.
QUEEN via the royal castle, KEY via 'keys to the castle'; the key side is a phrase rather than a first association.

best_available.why: The castle reaches the queen directly and the key through a familiar phrase.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; CITY is a clever alternative if the Queen City nickname is known to the audience.

hints.reason: KEY via the janitor's jangling bunch of keys, RING only via the ring those keys hang on; the ring side depends on the key side.
Contains both targets as substrings; rule failure.
KEY via key fob is immediate; RING is reached only because the fob hangs on a key ring.
KEY via keychain, RING via a chain being made of linked rings and the chain/ring pairing in jewelry; both sides reachable without the other.

best_available.why: Keychain is a broad compound and a chain is literally a run of rings.

pairs.pair_note: CHAIN is the one hint where the ring side stands on its own; JANITOR and FOB both route through 'key ring' and so lean on KEY.

hints.reason: ROBOT via the classic tin toy robot, KEY via the wind-up key in that toy's back; the key side only arrives through the toy.
Wind-up toy scene: you wind the key to make the toy robot walk.
KEY via key code or keypad code, ROBOT via the code that programs it.

best_available.why: The wind-up robot with a key in its back is a single familiar image.

pairs.pair_note: WIND is strongest; TIN relies on the same toy but makes the player supply the key.

hints.reason: Contains the target KEY as a substring; rule failure.
The fake hollow rock sold for hiding a spare key is one object that names both words.
Hiding the spare key under a rock is a familiar shared scene.

best_available.why: The hidden-key-under-a-rock scene is near-universal.

pairs.pair_note: Two solid scene hints; KEYSTONE falls to the substring rule.

hints.reason: KEY as a Florida island is fine, but SALT reaches ISLAND only via salt water, which is filler.
KEY via Key lime, SALT via the salt-and-lime of a tequila shot or margarita rim.
KEY via the Florida Keys is strong; SALT has no recognizable Florida link beyond generic sea water.

best_available.why: Key lime and salt-and-lime are both everyday pairings.

pairs.pair_note: LIME alone carries this pair; the two geography hints never reach SALT.

hints.reason: SHADOW via shadow play or shadow puppets, KEY via playing a key on a piano; the key side is a verb stretch.
KEY via skeleton key is strong; SHADOW reaches a skeleton only through generic spooky imagery.
SHADOW via shadow box (the display frame), KEY via a key box or lockbox; both are real compounds.
SHADOW via a shadowy figure, KEY via 'key figure' (an important person); both are common phrases.
KEY via door key is immediate; SHADOW has no distinctive route to a door.

best_available.why: Shadow box and key box are both established compound nouns.

pairs.pair_note: Two moderate passes; FIGURE relies on the phrase 'key figure' which some players may not surface.

hints.reason: KEY via the Florida Keys, SHARK via Florida's well-known shark waters and attacks.
KEY via Key West is strong; SHARK has no route to WEST.
KEY via Key Largo, but SHARK does not reach LARGO and the place name is niche.

best_available.why: Florida is home to the Keys and is widely associated with sharks.

pairs.pair_note: FLORIDA passes; the two Key place-names are one-sided.

hints.reason: SNAKE via the snake charmer, KEY via a keychain charm; the key side is lighter but recognizable.
SNAKE via the charmer's flute, KEY via the keys on a flute; both are real.
SNAKE via its scales, KEY via a musical scale in a key; two common senses of the hint.

best_available.why: Snake scales and a musical scale/key are both broad associations.

pairs.pair_note: All three pass; SCALE is the cleanest.

hints.reason: KEY via lock and key; SPIDER has no route to LOCK.
SPIDER via cobwebbed attics, KEY via the locked attic door key; the key side is plausible but weak.

best_available.why: A dusty locked attic is the one scene that includes both spiders and a key.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; the pair has little natural overlap.

hints.reason: Contains the target KEY as a substring; rule failure.
KEY via the Shift key is clear; STAR only via Shift+8 producing the asterisk, which needs explanation.
STAR via the asterisk being a little star symbol, KEY via the star/asterisk key on a phone keypad or keyboard.

best_available.why: The asterisk is a star shape and sits on a labelled key.

pairs.pair_note: ASTERISK passes moderately; SHIFT is the same idea one step removed.

hints.reason: TRAIN via train station; KEY has no direct route to a station.
KEY via locker key, TRAIN via the luggage lockers at a station; the train side is secondary.
Wind-up toy train scene: a key you wind to run the train.

best_available.why: The wind-up toy train with a key is a familiar object.

pairs.pair_note: WIND is the only pass; LOCKER is a fair second.

hints.reason: KEY as a small island (Florida Keys), WATER as what surrounds an island.
KEY via the Florida Keys is strong; WATER via Florida's coasts and beaches is a generic link.
KEY via 'low-key', WATER via low water or low tide; two common phrases.

best_available.why: Low-key and low water are both everyday phrases.

pairs.pair_note: LOW is the standout; ISLAND is fine, FLORIDA leans on KEY.

hints.reason: WITCH via a haunted house is spooky-adjacent; KEY has no route to HAUNTED.
KEY via locked doors; WITCH has no connection to LOCKED.
KEY via skeleton key, WITCH via skeletons and witches sharing Halloween imagery; the witch side is a scene association only.

best_available.why: Skeleton key is a strong compound and skeletons sit beside witches in Halloween decor.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; SKELETON is the only hint touching both sides.

hints.reason: KEY via lock and key; WOLF has no route to LOCK.
WOLF via Red Riding Hood's grandma is strong; KEY has no place in that story.
KEY via door key, WOLF via 'the wolf at the door' and the wolf knocking at the pigs' door.

best_available.why: Door key plus the wolf-at-the-door story image.

pairs.pair_note: DOOR passes cleanly; the other two are each wholly one-sided.

hints.reason: KNIGHT via the title Sir, KING via the monarch who dubs a knight 'Arise, Sir...'; one ceremony covers both.
King Arthur's Round Table and its knights.
King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table; one story names both.
Both are chess pieces.

best_available.why: Both words are literal chess pieces every player knows.

pairs.pair_note: Very strong pair; all four hints pass.

hints.reason: KING via The Lion King; LIGHT has no route to LION beyond a thrown-in film line.
KING via the crown; LIGHT does not reach CROWN.
LIGHT via sunlight, KING via the Sun King (Louis XIV) and the sun as king of the sky.

best_available.why: Sunlight is immediate and the Sun King is a widely known epithet.

pairs.pair_note: Only SUN reaches both; LION and CROWN are KING-only.

hints.reason: KING via The Lion King; MOON has no route to LION.
MOON via the night sky is immediate; KING reaches NIGHT only via the homophone knight, which is not a connection to KING itself.
MOON via crescent moon; KING has no link to CRESCENT.

best_available.why: Strongest moon side and the night/knight echo gives a faint royal flavour; still one-sided.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; none of the hints has a real KING route. A new hint is needed.

hints.reason: KING via The Lion King, MOUSE via Aesop's The Lion and the Mouse; two familiar stories.
The Nutcracker's villain is the Mouse King, which names both; the king side needs the player to know the ballet's plot.
KING via his castle, MOUSE via the Disney castle logo or a castle mouse; the mouse side is indirect.

best_available.why: Lion King plus the Lion and the Mouse fable are both widely known.

pairs.pair_note: LION is the safe serve; NUTCRACKER is more precise but depends on knowing the Mouse King.

hints.reason: KING via knights serving a king, NIGHT only via the homophone; a sound-alike is a thin route that the rubric does not list as valid.
Game of Thrones gives KING (kings and the Iron Throne) and NIGHT (the Night King, the Night's Watch); one show covers both.
KING via 'the King' Elvis; NIGHT has no clear route to Elvis.

best_available.why: Game of Thrones is widely known and contains both kings and the Night King.

pairs.pair_note: THRONES passes; KNIGHT is a homophone play worth an owner decision.

hints.reason: Poseidon is the king/god of the ocean.
KING via king crab, OCEAN via where crabs live.
King Triton of The Little Mermaid rules the sea; also the Greek sea god.
Neptune is the Roman king/god of the sea; same route as POSEIDON.

best_available.why: King of the sea is the direct meaning.

pairs.pair_note: All four pass; POSEIDON and NEPTUNE are the same idea twice.

hints.reason: PIRATE via pirate treasure, KING via the royal treasury and a king's hoard of treasure.
PIRATE via a letter of marque is niche and KING via the king who issued it is an explanation invented to rescue the word.
KING via the crown; PIRATE has no route to CROWN beyond a 'pirate king' trope.

best_available.why: Treasure belongs to both pirates and kings in ordinary story imagery.

pairs.pair_note: TREASURE is the only pass.

hints.reason: King-size and queen-size beds.
King and queen are both face cards.
Both sit on a throne.
Shared property: both are royals; broad but accurate for both.
Both are chess pieces.

best_available.why: King and queen bed sizes are the most everyday pairing that does not also point at other royals.

pairs.pair_note: Every hint passes; the pair is almost too easy.

hints.reason: Kissing the king's ring is one scene of fealty that names both.
Aragorn is the returning King in The Lord of the Rings.
KING Solomon is broadly known, but the Ring/Seal of Solomon is a niche legend.
A signet ring is the king's seal ring; both words live in the compound.

best_available.why: Signet ring is the object itself and it is a royal emblem.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes of moderate recognizability; SOLOMON is too niche on the ring side.

hints.reason: ROBOT via RoboCop; KING has no route.
KING via the throne; ROBOT has no route.
KING via the chess piece, ROBOT via chess computers like Deep Blue beating humans; the robot side is a stretch.

best_available.why: The only hint with any robot side, through chess-playing machines.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; the pair needs a new hint.

hints.reason: ROCK via rock and roll, KING via the King of Rock and Roll; the king side arrives through the same phrase.
The Lion King's Pride Rock covers both; also lions are kings of beasts.
Both sides route through The Lion King (Pride Rock, the pride's king), so the player must find the film first.
Elvis is 'the King' of rock and roll.

best_available.why: The King of rock is a single widely known epithet.

pairs.pair_note: Good pair; PRIDE is a weaker echo of LION.

hints.reason: Tudor kings (Henry VIII) and the Tudor rose emblem.
ROSE via rose garden; KING has no route to GARDEN.
The Wars of the Roses were fought between rival claimants to the English crown; both sides depend on knowing that history.

best_available.why: The Tudor rose and Tudor kings are a tight historical pairing.

pairs.pair_note: Two history-based passes; GARDEN is one-sided.

hints.reason: SALT via the salt tax (Gandhi's Salt March), KING via the king's taxes; shared historical theme.
KING Midas is strong; SALT has no route (Midas turned things to gold, not salt).
KING Lear is known; the 'love like salt' folk-tale cousin of the Lear story is far too obscure to reach SALT.

best_available.why: Salt taxes and royal taxes are both recognizable history.

pairs.pair_note: TAX is the only pass; the two named kings never reach SALT.

hints.reason: KING via The Lion King, SHADOW only via the film's 'shadowy place' / shadowlands line, which a player must recall.
KING via the throne; SHADOW has no route.
KING only via Scar being the usurper in The Lion King, and SHADOW has no route at all.

best_available.why: Only hint with any shadow side, through the Lion King's shadowlands.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; all three lean on The Lion King and none reaches SHADOW well.

hints.reason: SHARK via apex predator, KING via the king as the apex of a hierarchy; the king side is a shared-property stretch.
KING via king mackerel, SHARK via mackerel sharks or sharks eating mackerel; both are fishing-trivia routes.
SHARK via the ocean, KING via the shark as king of the ocean; the king side only exists as a description of the shark.

best_available.why: Apex predator is a strong shark link and 'apex' as top-of-hierarchy reaches king more honestly than OCEAN does.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; every hint is a shared-property stretch on the KING side.

hints.reason: KING via pharaoh as Egypt's king, SNAKE via the cobra on the pharaoh's crown and the asp of Cleopatra.
Contains both targets as substrings; rule failure.
SNAKE via The Jungle Book's Kaa; KING has no route (King Louie is a different character).
King cobra is a common compound and a cobra is a snake.

best_available.why: King cobra is the most widely known compound for this pair.
